## Introduction

Starting in 2023 Netflix started publishing What We Watched reports to give advertisers and creators a better understanding of what consumers watch. The reports come out every six months and list how many hours each title was viewed, and this project covers the first half of 2023 through the first half of 2026. We clean the data, explore patterns and trends, and finish with a memo for Netflix on what to focus on in the future.

## Data Acquisition and Preparation

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

#' Acquire Netflix What We Watched Reports
#'
#' This function will acquire and standardize all data for MP#01
#' from Netflix. Because Netflix hosts the data files behind a CDN, we
#' are accessing the release pages and automatically extracting links to the
#' relevant files (with CDN hash).
#'
#' After import, files are stacked vertically and some basic cleaning is
#' performed.
load_netflix_data <- function(){
  library(tidyverse)
  library(rvest)
  library(readxl)
  library(fs)
  
  data_dir <- path("data", "mp01")
  
  if(!dir_exists(data_dir)){
    dir_create(data_dir, showWarnings=FALSE, recurse=TRUE)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )
  
  download_if_needed <- function(url, local){
    if(!file_exists(local)){
      download.file(url, local, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
    }
  
    return(local)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS |>
    map(read_html) |>
    map(html_element, xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]") |>
    map_chr(html_attr, "href") |>
    enframe("period", "url") |>
   mutate(path = path(data_dir, paste0(period, ".xlsx")),
          path = map2(url, path, download_if_needed),
          data = map(path, read_excel, skip=3, na="*"),
          data = map(data, \(x) x |> mutate(`Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)))) |>
    unnest(data) |>
    select(-url, -path) |>
    mutate(year=str_sub(period, 1, 4),
           half=str_sub(period, start=6),
           period_start = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 1, 7), 1),
           period_end = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 6, 12), if_else(half==1, 30, 31))) |>
    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |>
    mutate(live_event = !is.na(Runtime) & str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"),
           clean_time = str_remove(Runtime, fixed("*")),
           Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) + minute(hm(clean_time))) |>
    select(-clean_time) |>
    mutate(Runtime = coalesce(Runtime, mean(Runtime, na.rm=TRUE)),
           .by=Title,
           Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(Title, "Latin-ASCII"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, " // .*"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, "[^[:ascii:]].*"),
           Title = str_trim(Title)) |>
    filter_out(Title == "") |>
    select(year,
           period,
           period_start,
           period_end,
           Title,
           -half,
           Runtime,
           Views,
           `Hours Viewed`,
           `Release Date`,
           `Available Globally?`,
           live_event)
}

NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data()
```

```{r}
# Task 2: rename columns to tidy snake_case names
# Task 3: convert year to integer and global availability to TRUE/FALSE
NETFLIX_DATA <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  rename(
    title              = Title,
    runtime            = Runtime,
    views              = Views,
    hours_viewed       = `Hours Viewed`,
    release_date       = `Release Date`,
    available_globally = `Available Globally?`
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year               = as.integer(year),
    available_globally = available_globally == "Yes"
  )
```

## Exploratory Analysis

### Initial Data Checks

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
glimpse(NETFLIX_DATA)
```

The data has 61,892 rows and 11 columns, each row is one title in a one six-month period. After the cleaning in Task 3, the column types are correct: year is now an integer, the date columns are stored as real dates, and available_globally is now TRUE/FALSE. One thing to flag is that views shows NA for the first rows, because those are from the first half of 2023 and that report didn't include views.

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
library(skimr)
skim(NETFLIX_DATA)
```

The skim output shows that hours_viewed has no missing values. Views are missing for 29% of rows, which matches the first half of 2023 gap, runtime is missing for 21% of rows, and release_date is missing for 57%, so release dates aren't reliable. Hours viewed had a mean of 8.3M and a median of only 1.8M, so the data was skewed.

### Exploratory Questions

```{r}
library(scales)

# Q1: date range covered
date_start <- min(NETFLIX_DATA$period_start)
date_end   <- max(NETFLIX_DATA$period_end)

# Q2: number of distinct titles
n_titles <- n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$title)

# Q3: Bridgerton universe hours
bridgerton_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Bridgerton")) |>
  summarize(total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total)

# Q4: the five main Stranger Things seasons only
stranger_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Stranger Things")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Beyond")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Tales")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Fireplace")) |>
  summarize(total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total)

# Q5: share of 2026H1 watch time captured by its top 10 titles
h1_2026     <- NETFLIX_DATA |> filter(period == "2026H1")
top10_share <- h1_2026 |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 10) |>
  summarize(share = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(share) / sum(h1_2026$hours_viewed)

# Q6: share of catalog available globally, by title and by hours
global_by_title <- mean(NETFLIX_DATA$available_globally, na.rm = TRUE)
global_by_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(!is.na(available_globally)) |>
  summarize(share = sum(hours_viewed[available_globally]) / sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(share)
```

1. The range covered in this data is `r format(date_start, "%B %d, %Y")` to `r format(date_end, "%B %d, %Y")`.
2. There are `r comma(n_titles)` different shows and movies in this data set.
3. There have been `r comma(bridgerton_hours)` total hours watched in the Bridgerton universe.
4. There have been `r comma(stranger_hours)` total hours spent watching the five seasons of Stranger Things.
5. In the first half of 2026, the top 10 titles accounted for `r percent(top10_share, 0.1)` of all viewing.
6. Of all titles in Netflix's catalog, `r percent(global_by_title, 0.1)` are globally available. These titles account for `r percent(global_by_hours, 0.1)` of total hours viewed.

### Exploratory Tables

```{r}
#| message: false
library(gt)
SOURCE_NOTE <- "Source: Netflix 'What We Watched' engagement reports, 2023H1–2026H1."
```

#### Top Title in Each Period

```{r}
# Task 6.1: top title per period and its share of that period's total hours
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(period_total = sum(hours_viewed), .by = period) |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 1, by = period, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  transmute(period, title, hours_viewed,
            share = hours_viewed / period_total) |>
  arrange(period) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Top Netflix Title in Each Six-Month Period",
             subtitle = "Ranked by total hours viewed") |>
  cols_label(period = "Period", title = "Title",
             hours_viewed = "Hours Viewed",
             share = "Share of Period Viewing") |>
  fmt_number(hours_viewed, suffixing = TRUE, decimals = 1) |>
  fmt_percent(share, decimals = 2) |>
  tab_source_note(SOURCE_NOTE)
```

Table 1 shows the top title in each period and the share of viewing hours it got. The number one title gets around 1% of the viewing in each period. The share did go up over time from 0.87% to a high of 1.35% . This shows that the biggest hits are getting bigger than they were before. Returning seasons also took 5 of the 7 number one spots, and Squid Game Season 2 was number one for two periods in a row, which shows that a returning hit can keep its momentum going.

#### Catalog Size Over Time


```{r}
# Task 6.2: number of titles and total runtime per period
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(n_titles      = n_distinct(title),
            runtime_hours = sum(runtime, na.rm = TRUE) / 60,
            .by = period) |>
  arrange(period) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Size of Netflix's Reported Catalog by Period",
             subtitle = "Number of titles and total runtime of content") |>
  cols_label(period = "Period", n_titles = "Number of Titles",
             runtime_hours = "Total Runtime (Hours)") |>
  fmt_number(n_titles, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(runtime_hours, suffixing = TRUE, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_source_note(SOURCE_NOTE) |>
  tab_source_note("Runtime excludes titles with no published runtime (about 21% of rows).")
```

Table 2 shows the number of titles and total runtime in each period. The big drop from 18,126 titles to around 6,500 is a data issue and not a real drop, since Netflix split its reports into TV and Film tabs after the first half of 2023 and only TV was loaded. From the second half of 2023 on, the catalog grew from 6,574 to 8,163 titles, about 24%. This shows Netflix is still adding more content over time.

#### Most Consistent "Comfort Food" Titles


```{r}
# Task 6.3: titles present in every period, ranked by their worst period.
# A high minimum means the title never had a weak period; a low
# coefficient of variation (sd / mean) means viewing was steady.
n_periods_total <- n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$period)

NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(n_periods = n_distinct(period),
            avg_hours = mean(hours_viewed),
            min_hours = min(hours_viewed),
            sd_hours  = sd(hours_viewed),
            .by = title) |>
  filter(n_periods == n_periods_total) |>
  mutate(cv = sd_hours / avg_hours) |>
  slice_max(min_hours, n = 10) |>
  select(title, avg_hours, min_hours, cv) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Netflix's Most Consistent Titles",
             subtitle = "Titles in all seven periods, ranked by their lowest period") |>
  cols_label(title = "Title", avg_hours = "Avg. Hours per Period",
             min_hours = "Lowest Period (Hours)",
             cv = "Variability (CV)") |>
  fmt_number(c(avg_hours, min_hours), suffixing = TRUE, decimals = 1) |>
  fmt_number(cv, decimals = 2) |>
  tab_source_note(SOURCE_NOTE) |>
  tab_source_note("CV = standard deviation / mean; lower values mean steadier viewership.")
```

Table 3 shows the titles with the most consistent viewership. Consistent is when a title shows up in all of the 7 periods. Then rank them by their weakest period so one big spike wouldn’t skew the data. CV measures how much a title’s viewing moves around between periods, lower is steadier. Findings of steady shows like Breaking Bad and Money Heist had a CV of around 0.12 to 0.17.

#### Shows vs. Movies


```{r}
# Task 6.4: classify titles. Live events are their own category; otherwise
# a title is a show if it has "Season", "Series", or "Limited" in the name
# or runs longer than 4 hours (240 minutes); everything else is a movie.
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(type = case_when(
    live_event ~ "Live Event",
    str_detect(title, "Season|Series|Limited") ~ "Show",
    coalesce(runtime > 240, FALSE) ~ "Show",
    TRUE ~ "Movie")) |>
  summarize(hours = sum(hours_viewed), .by = c(period, type)) |>
  mutate(share = hours / sum(hours), .by = period) |>
  select(period, type, share) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = type, values_from = share, values_fill = 0) |>
  arrange(period) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Share of Viewing Time: Shows vs. Movies",
             subtitle = "Percent of each period's total hours viewed") |>
  cols_label(period = "Period") |>
  fmt_percent(-period, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_source_note(SOURCE_NOTE) |>
  tab_source_note("Shows: titles containing 'Season', 'Series', or 'Limited', or longer than 4 hours.")
```

Table 4 shows the share of viewing that went to shows vs. movies in each period. A title was counted as a show if it had “Season,” “Series,” or “Limited” in the title, or a runtime over 4 hours. Only the first half of 2023 gives a real split, around 71% shows and 29% movies, later periods only had Tv loaded.


#### Live Events vs. Pre-Taped Content

```{r}
# Task 6.5: average and top-tier performance of live vs pre-taped content.
# Views (hours / runtime) adjusts for length, since live events are short.
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(type = if_else(live_event, "Live Event", "Pre-Taped")) |>
  summarize(n_entries  = n(),
            avg_hours  = mean(hours_viewed),
            avg_views  = mean(views, na.rm = TRUE),
            top10_hours = mean(head(sort(hours_viewed, decreasing = TRUE), 10)),
            top10_views = mean(head(sort(views, decreasing = TRUE), 10)),
            .by = type) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Live Events vs. Pre-Taped Content",
             subtitle = "Average title vs. top-10 titles in each group") |>
  cols_label(type = "Content Type", n_entries = "Entries",
             avg_hours = "Avg. Hours", avg_views = "Avg. Views",
             top10_hours = "Top-10 Avg. Hours",
             top10_views = "Top-10 Avg. Views") |>
  fmt_number(n_entries, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(-c(type, n_entries), suffixing = TRUE, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_source_note(SOURCE_NOTE) |>
  tab_source_note("Views are Netflix's estimate (hours viewed / runtime); unavailable for 2023H1.")
```

Table 5 compares live events to pre-taped titles. By hours, live looks weak because live events are usually short. When compared by views they are almost equal, 1.5M for live and 1.4M for pre-taped. At the top shows vs live events it is different, the biggest pre-taped titles get about 9 times more views than the biggest live events, 106.3M vs 11.3M.


## Final Insights and Deliverable

```{r}
#| message: false
# Numbers used in the strategy memo

# Topic 1: global vs regional titles
global_trend <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(!is.na(available_globally)) |>
  summarize(share_titles = mean(available_globally),
            share_hours  = sum(hours_viewed[available_globally]) / sum(hours_viewed),
            .by = period)
global_hours_first <- global_trend |> filter(period == "2023H2") |> pull(share_hours)
global_hours_last  <- global_trend |> filter(period == "2026H1") |> pull(share_hours)

# Topic 2: live events
live_trend <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(live_share = sum(hours_viewed[live_event]) / sum(hours_viewed),
            .by = period)
live_share_last  <- live_trend |> filter(period == "2026H1") |> pull(live_share)
live_avg_views   <- mean(NETFLIX_DATA$views[NETFLIX_DATA$live_event], na.rm = TRUE)
tape_avg_views   <- mean(NETFLIX_DATA$views[!NETFLIX_DATA$live_event], na.rm = TRUE)
live_top10_views <- mean(head(sort(NETFLIX_DATA$views[NETFLIX_DATA$live_event], decreasing = TRUE), 10))
tape_top10_views <- mean(head(sort(NETFLIX_DATA$views[!NETFLIX_DATA$live_event], decreasing = TRUE), 10))

global_titles_last <- global_trend |> filter(period == "2026H1") |> pull(share_titles)
live_views_lift    <- live_avg_views / tape_avg_views - 1
top10_gap          <- tape_top10_views / live_top10_views

# Topic 3: returning franchises
# A title counts as "returning" if it is Season 2 or later
# (e.g. "Season 3") or a numbered sequel (e.g. "Stranger Things 4")
is_returning <- function(t) str_detect(t, "Season ([2-9]|[1-9][0-9])|\\s[2-9]$")

top1_titles <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 1, by = period, with_ties = FALSE)
n_top1_returning <- sum(is_returning(top1_titles$title))
n_periods        <- nrow(top1_titles)

top10_titles <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 10, by = period, with_ties = FALSE)
top10_returning_share <- mean(is_returning(top10_titles$title))

top1_by_period <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(share = hours_viewed / sum(hours_viewed), .by = period) |>
  slice_max(share, n = 1, by = period, with_ties = FALSE)
top1_first <- top1_by_period |> filter(period == "2023H1") |> pull(share)
top1_peak  <- max(top1_by_period$share)

```

**To:** Netflix Leadership  
**From:** Waseem Gazali  
**Date:** October 2026  
**Subject:** Netflix content strategy for 2027 and beyond

Netflix’s What We Watched reports from 2023-2026 revealed a meaningful path forward for Netflix in 2027 and onward. Global titles appear to be more efficient releases than regional titles. Another point is that returning seasons of series remain the most reliable way to claim the top spots. Even as new titles are still able to fill up the rest of the top ten, returning titles find their way frequently. Lastly, live events are holding their weight compared to the average pre-taped title, but the biggest live events remain much smaller than the biggest scripted shows. Live events have their place in Netflix’s ecosystem, but a more directed output could yield better results for the company.

### Global Content

Global titles make up `r percent(global_titles_last, 0.1)` of the catalog and account for `r percent(global_hours_last, 0.1)` of all viewing hours. This means that they earn significantly more viewing per title than regional titles. Their share of total viewing hours declined from `r percent(global_hours_first, 0.1)` in the second half of 2023 to `r percent(global_hours_last, 0.1)` in the first half of 2026. We saw King the Land reach the number one spot despite being regional. Regional content is gaining momentum, but the gap is still significant. Some of the biggest successes like Squid Game and Money Heist show the strength of titles released with global reach. Breakout titles with room to grow spread quickly. Netflix should prioritize more of these titles since great titles are enjoyed worldwide and can be held back by regional locks.

### Returning Franchises

Returning seasons claimed `r n_top1_returning` of `r n_periods` number one spots, including the Bridgerton titles, Squid Game titles, and Wednesday titles. The only new titles to reach the number one spot were The Night Agent and King the Land. Returning seasons made up `r percent(top10_returning_share, 1)` of top ten slots, so new shows still occupy most of those slots. The number one title is also getting bigger over time, it went from `r percent(top1_first, 0.01)` to `r percent(top1_peak, 0.01)`, so having a strong returning series is becoming more valuable as time goes. The Stranger Things series has `r comma(stranger_hours)` hours since they ran so this shows that these returning titles keep paying off for a substantial time. Squid Games was also a perfect example of this, a global breakout that held the number one spot for two consecutive periods and can continuously be built on as a returning franchise. For 2027 Netflix should continue with successful series but still keep launching enough new titles to create the next generation of these continuing seasons.

### Live Events

Live events accounted for `r percent(live_share_last, 0.1)` of viewing hours in the first half of 2026. On average a live event drew `r comma(live_avg_views)` views while a pre-taped title drew `r comma(tape_avg_views)`. But when you compare the biggest live events with the biggest pre-taped titles, the gap is much bigger. The top pre-taped titles reach `r round(top10_gap, 1)` times more views than the largest live events, `r comma(tape_top10_views)` for pre-taped and `r comma(live_top10_views)` for live. Netflix should grow the category in a more focused way. The events already hold their weight against ordinary titles and clearly belong in the mix, but their lower ceiling argues for a focused route rather than a broad expansion.

### Conclusion

Looking ahead, Netflix should build and keep emphasis on global titles as momentum has shown how massive a global title can reach. Also, Netflix should keep live events focused and targeted rather than expansive. Lastly, proven titles have shown that it is worth investing in returning seasons for them, but it is still important to keep the pipeline of new titles going so new opportunities for franchise building can arise. No single title can carry a substantial amount of viewing, so a wide catalog is important for Netflix. The data shows consumer interests for Netflix to cater to. It also shows areas where Netflix can reassess market goals and use resources wisely. Overall consumers are providing traceable feedback with glimpses and signs of what is working and what isn’t.
